solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Can't I free zebra in captivity? This will encourage better running in extreme temperatures

definitions.text: This will encourage better running in extreme temperatures

indicators.note: something held in captivity is locked up inside, so the answer is confined within these words

explanation.surface: A plea to release a caged zebra, followed by a remark about running in extreme heat or cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters run across 'can't I free zebra', held 'in captivity' by those words; the long definition reads like a comment about the zebra running, but it is about engines.
explanation.definitionFit: Antifreeze added to an engine's coolant stops it freezing, so the motor keeps running well in bitter cold.

clue.text: Wasted hours in support

indicators.note: something wasted is ruined or wrecked, so these letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Time frittered away while supposedly helping someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' signals rearranging the letters of HOURS and IN together.
explanation.definitionFit: To nourish is to sustain or feed, so it means support in the sense of keeping something alive and growing.

clue.text: Current price makes you angry

parts.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current
a rate is a price or charge

explanation.surface: Today's price is enough to make a shopper furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like 'present-day' but stands for I, the symbol for electric current.
explanation.definitionFit: Irate is a straightforward synonym, describing someone furious or incensed.

clue.text: 70s rock band on time for jam session?

parts.note: Rush were a Canadian progressive rock trio who made their name in the 1970s
an hour is a unit of time

explanation.surface: A classic rock group turning up punctually to play together.
explanation.walkthrough: A jam session sounds musical, fitting the band, but here the jam is traffic: the busy period when roads clog.
explanation.definitionFit: The commuting peak is when traffic jams form, so the question mark lets the period be called a session of jams.

clue.text: Extremely important and possibly heart breaking

indicators.note: possibly says the word heart could be arranged another way

parts.note: shattering means breaking into pieces

explanation.surface: Something momentous that might also cause heartbreak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart breaking' looks like one word split in two, but 'possibly' scrambles only the first word and 'breaking' is a synonym in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth-shattering describes news or events of enormous consequence, momentous enough to shake the world.

clue.text: Times to put in record and increase the volume

indicators.note: the multiplication sign is to be placed inside the short record

parts.note: EP is an extended-play record
X is the multiplication sign, read as times
taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions to add tracks to a record and turn it up louder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' is not the newspaper but X, the times sign; 'increase the volume' suggests loudness but means grow in size.
explanation.definitionFit: To expand is to grow larger, increasing in bulk or size.

clue.text: Page leaves gem for nobleman

indicators.note: leaves means goes away from, so the page's abbreviation departs from the jewel

parts.note: a pearl is a gem

explanation.surface: A young page servant walks away from a precious stone meant for a lord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Page' looks like a servant in the noble household, but it is just the letter P.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is a British peer, ranking above a viscount and below a marquess.

clue.text: A nice G&T and I'm turning mysterious

indicators.note: turning, as in turning over, says these letters are shifted into a fresh order

parts.note: G and T are the letters of the gin and tonic abbreviation, without the ampersand

explanation.surface: A drinker's head spins after a gin and tonic, leaving them puzzled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning' rearranges A, NICE, GT and IM; 'and' is only a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: Enigmatic describes something puzzling or inscrutable, like a riddle.

clue.text: Following advance drops in fares one owed what's left

indicators.note: drops means lets fall away, so those two letters leave the word fares

parts.note: A is taken as an abbreviation for advance
I is the Roman numeral one
due means owed

explanation.surface: After an advance payment, falling fares leave a traveller still owing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops' takes F (following) and A (advance) out of the word fares; A for advance is a rare abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A residue is the remainder left over after something has been removed or used.

clue.text: Back at college and adult cuddles male cat

indicators.note: cuddles means holds close, so the male's letter is wrapped inside the rest
back says the short word for being at college is turned round

parts.note: up means at university, as in up at Oxford
A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: A student returns to college, and a grown-up hugs a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns the college word round, and 'cuddles' wraps the result plus A around M. Being 'up' at college is a British usage, from going up to Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The puma, also called the cougar or mountain lion, is a large wild feline of the Americas.

clue.text: Stop priest getting drunk and most quarrelsome

indicators.note: getting drunk suggests staggering about, so these letters lurch into a new order

explanation.surface: A clergyman is told to stop drinking before he turns belligerent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting drunk' rearranges the letters of STOP PRIEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Stroppy is British slang for bad-tempered and argumentative, so the superlative means the most cantankerous.

clue.text: Catch surrounding ultimate in house furnishing style

indicators.note: surrounding means one piece is placed around another

parts.note: a hitch is a catch, a snag or difficulty

indicators.note: ultimate in means the final letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A snag around the final details of decorating a home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimate in house' gives E, which HITCH (a catch) goes 'surrounding'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hi-tech is an interior design style using industrial materials and fittings in the home.

clue.text: It could describe antique, servant declared

indicators.note: declared means spoken out, so the word for servant is heard rather than spelled

parts.note: a handmaid is a female servant

explanation.surface: A servant speaks up about an antique.
explanation.walkthrough: A HANDMAID, an old word for a maidservant, is said aloud, giving a word that describes many antiques.
explanation.definitionFit: An antique is often made by craftsmen rather than machines, so the word could describe it.

clue.text: Finished eating — one's initially full

indicators.note: eating means taking in, so one piece swallows another

parts.note: through means finished, as in 'I'm through with this'

indicators.note: initially picks the opening letter of the word after

explanation.surface: A diner has stopped eating and is feeling full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's initially' gives O, which THROUGH (finished) is 'eating'; 'full' looks like the diner's state but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorough means complete and exhaustive, so 'full' as in a full investigation.

clue.text: Shot hit grouse, just

indicators.note: shot means broken or ruined, so these letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A hunter's shot has just hit a game bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' rearranges HIT GROUSE; 'just' looks like 'only now' but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Righteous means morally upright and fair, matching just as an adjective.

clue.text: Pour me last bit of coffee — tense when returning

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the assembled letters are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: last bit of picks the closing letter of the word that follows

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Someone asks for the dregs of the coffee, feeling tense as they come back.
explanation.walkthrough: ME, E (the end of coffee) and T together are turned round 'when returning'; 'Pour' looks like an instruction to serve coffee but means rain heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: To teem is to rain heavily, as in 'it's pouring down'.

clue.text: Caught artist turning on amusing lamp

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means one piece sits above the other
turning means the artist's abbreviation is flipped round

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
light means amusing, as in light entertainment

explanation.surface: A painter is caught switching on a funny lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning' gives AR from RA; with C that makes ARC, and 'on' puts it above LIGHT. The blog reverses C plus RA together, which also gives ARC.
explanation.definitionFit: An arc light is a brilliant electric lamp producing light from an arc between electrodes.

clue.text: Smirking son kisses face

indicators.note: kisses means touches, so the son's letter sits right against the next piece

parts.note: mug is slang for face

explanation.surface: A self-satisfied boy kisses someone's face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kisses' puts S right next to MUG.
explanation.definitionFit: Smug describes someone looking complacently self-satisfied, which is what a smirk shows.

clue.text: This setter has a certain standard

parts.note: crossword setters refer to themselves as me
sure means certain

explanation.surface: The compiler boasts of a reliable level of quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This setter' is the compiler speaking of themselves, giving ME; 'has' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: A measure is a standard of comparison or yardstick used for judging.

clue.text: Renegade to direct film

parts.note: to turn something is to direct it, as in turning attention to a task
a coat is a thin film or layer, as of paint

explanation.surface: Someone defects in order to direct a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' suggests cinema but means a thin layer, COAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A turncoat is a traitor who switches sides, just as a renegade deserts a cause.

clue.text: Country woman's after a male

indicators.note: after says the woman's name comes behind the other pieces

parts.note: Erica is a woman's name; the 's stands for 'is'

explanation.surface: A rural woman pursuing a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country woman' looks like a description of a farm girl, but 'Country' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: America is commonly used for the United States, a country.

clue.text: Notebook — the fellow stores one in automobile

indicators.note: in places the combined pieces inside the vehicle

parts.note: a car is an automobile

indicators.note: stores means keeps inside, so the numeral is held within the man

parts.note: he refers to the fellow
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A man keeps a notebook in his car.
explanation.walkthrough: HE 'stores' I, making HIE, which goes 'in' CAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Cahier is a French word adopted in English for an exercise book or notebook.

clue.text: Clothes-line

parts.note: read not as a washing line but as a line of business, the one that deals in clothes

explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated word suggests drying laundry; the second reading treats line as a line of work.
explanation.definitionFit: The clothing industry is informally called this, so it is the business line concerned with garments.

clue.text: Jumped with power and energy into first place

indicators.note: into means the two letters go inside the other piece

parts.note: the lead is first place in a race
P is the physics symbol for power
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A runner surged with strength and vigour into the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: P and E go 'into' LEAD; 'with' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaped is a past tense of leap, meaning jumped.

clue.text: John kept by a female at arm's length

indicators.note: kept by means held inside, so the toilet is enclosed by the other pieces

parts.note: john is slang for a toilet, and loo is the British word for one

explanation.surface: A man named John is kept at a distance by a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John' looks like a man's name but is slang for a toilet, LOO.
explanation.definitionFit: Aloof means reserved and distant, keeping others at arm's length.

clue.text: Extolling European Union — Liberal is going to get hammered

indicators.note: to get hammered means to be beaten out of shape, so these letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Praising the EU while a Liberal is off to get drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hammered' looks like British slang for drunk, but here it rearranges the letters of IS GOING.
explanation.definitionFit: Eulogising means praising highly, as in delivering a eulogy; it is the British spelling.

clue.text: Leave out books with note in

indicators.note: in means the musical note goes inside the books

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of books
mi is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Instructions to leave out books with a note tucked inside.
explanation.walkthrough: MI goes 'in' OT; 'with' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: To omit is to leave something out or exclude it.

clue.text: Encourages amateur to quit plays

indicators.note: to quit means to leave, so the amateur's letter goes away

parts.note: abets means encourages or helps

explanation.surface: Someone urges a novice to give up acting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Encourages' looks like the definition but gives ABETS; 'plays' is the definition, in the sense of gambles.
explanation.definitionFit: Plays means gambles or wagers, as in plays the horses.

clue.text: Designated track — why I got far when rambling?

indicators.note: rambling means wandering about, so the letters stray into a new order

explanation.surface: A walker wonders why they covered such distance on a ramble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When rambling' rearranges WHY I GOT FAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A right-of-way is a path the public is legally allowed to use across land.
